Questions
This notebook uses the record of North Atlantic tropical cyclones kept by the U.S. National Hurricane Center. A row is not a storm. It is one observation of one storm at one moment: where the center of the storm was (lon and lat, in degrees), how fast its winds were blowing (wind, in knots), what Saffir-Simpson category it had reached, and a two-letter status code, where TD is a tropical depression, TS a tropical storm, and HU a hurricane. The remaining status codes describe systems that are not quite tropical. Positions are logged every six hours, so a storm that lasts a week leaves behind about thirty rows. The columns year, month, day, and hour give the time of the observation, and doy gives the day of the year, counting from 1 on the first of January.
Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it to a variable.

Make a scatter plot of all 25,112 observations with longitude on the x-axis and latitude on the y-axis.



View code
(
    storm
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)









Nothing in that code knows what a map is, and yet the outline of one is there. The points fan out from the tropics on the lower left, bunch up over the Gulf and the Caribbean, and drift northeast into the open Atlantic, which is the path storms take. The middle of the plot is a solid black mass, so this is the last plot we can read this way.

There are too many points to follow any single storm. Plot the same two columns again, but only for the 2005 season, which produced 688 observations across 21 named storms.



View code

    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)










One of those 2005 storms was Katrina. Filter down to the rows where name is "Katrina" and plot the track. The result is not one storm. What happened?



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.name == "Katrina")
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)









Answer: The filter returns 70 rows describing three different storms. The Hurricane Center recycles names on a six-year rotation, so a name is reused until a storm is bad enough to have its name retired. There was a Katrina in 1981 and another in 1999 before the one in 2005. To identify a storm you need both the name and the year.

Fix the previous plot by filtering on the name and the year at once. You should be left with 34 observations.



View code

    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)









Now the shape of the storm’s path is clear. Katrina formed near the Bahamas, crossed the southern tip of Florida, turned northwest into the Gulf of Mexico, and came ashore in Louisiana before running up into the Ohio valley.

The plot above shows where Katrina went but says nothing about how strong it was. Using the same two filters, plot the day of the year on the x-axis and the wind speed on the y-axis.



View code

    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.doy, c.wind))
    .geom_point()
)









The whole life of the storm took nine days, from day 235 to day 243. It strengthened slowly, crossed Florida, then doubled in strength in about forty-eight hours over the warm water of the Gulf, peaking at 150 knots. The collapse on the right of the plot is landfall. Each point is a separate reading taken six hours after the last one, which is why they are evenly spaced. Drawing a line between them is the obvious next thing to want, and it is the first thing we will do next class.

View code
storm = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/storms.csv")




Questions
We are staying with the North Atlantic storms from last time. Each row is one observation of one storm at one moment, taken every six hours, with the position of the storm’s center (lon, lat), its wind speed in knots (wind), its Saffir-Simpson category, a two-letter status code, and the name and year that together identify which storm it belongs to. The column doy gives the day of the year.
Last time we had only one geometry and one color of point. This notebook adds the rest of the layer: the aesthetics that carry extra columns into the plot, and the geometries other than points.
Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it to a variable.

Plot the tracks of the 2005 season again, longitude against latitude, but map the name column to the color aesthetic so that each storm gets its own color. Remember that every aesthetic other than x and y goes inside a second call to aes(), placed inside the geometry.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.name))
)









Last week these 688 points were an anonymous tangle. One aesthetic separates them into 21 storms, and the legend tells you which is which.

A color can also be set to a fixed value rather than mapped to a column, and the same is true of alpha, which controls how transparent each point is. Recall that the very first plot of the last notebook, all 25,112 observations at once, came out as a solid black mass. Draw it again with alpha fixed at 0.05.



View code
(
    storm
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.05)
)









Twenty points must now stack up before the ink is fully black, so the darkness of a region tells you how many storms have passed through it. The corridor from the Caribbean through the Gulf is the darkest part of the plot. You can also pick out the storms that form off the coast of Africa on the right and run west across the open ocean, and the pale fan at the top where the survivors curve away to the northeast and die in the cold water.
Note the syntax: alpha=0.05 sits inside geom_point() but outside aes(). A value inside aes() is a column name; a value outside it is a constant. This is the single most common mistake people make with this package.

Map the color aesthetic to category instead, for the 2005 season. The legend comes out looking quite different from the one in question 1. Why?



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.category))
)









Answer: The legend is a continuous color bar rather than a list of labeled swatches, because category has type i64. The package looks at the type of the column, sees a number, and assumes the values fall on a scale where 4 lies between 3 and 5. It cannot know that there are only seven possible values and that they are really labels. With name, a str, it had no choice but to treat each value as a separate group.

The fix is a cast, from Chapter 3. Convert category to a string inside .with_columns() before you plot it, and compare the result with question 3.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .with_columns(category = c.category.cast(pl.String))
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.category))
)









Seven discrete colors, one legend entry each. It is easier now to see that the strongest parts of a storm happen in short bursts: most of every track is dark purple, and the two or three days at category 4 or 5 are a small bright stretch in the middle. The type of a column decides what the plot looks like.

The 2005 season is famous for having exhausted the alphabet, and the plot shows where it spent itself. Most of these storms peaked in the Gulf of Mexico or the Caribbean, packed into the left half of the plot. Only four peaked east of 60 degrees, and one of them, Vince, is out near the coast of Portugal at longitude -19, which is a strange place for a hurricane to be.
The crowding on the left is the weakness of this geometry. Katrina and Arlene peaked close enough together that their labels collide, and Jose, Bret, and Stan are piled on top of one another in the Bay of Campeche. Nudging helps, but it cannot untangle labels that genuinely overlap. The honest fix is usually to label fewer things, which is what question 11 does.

Back to a single storm. In the last notebook we plotted Katrina’s wind speed against the day of the year and said that connecting the points was the obvious next thing to want. Do that now with geom_line.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.doy, c.wind))
    .geom_line()
)










The line geometry takes a color aesthetic just as the point geometry does. Plot wind against day of the year for the four strongest storms of 2005, Dennis, Katrina, Rita, and Wilma, with one colored line each.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .filter(c.name.is_in(["Dennis", "Katrina", "Rita", "Wilma"]))
    .ggplot(aes(c.doy, c.wind))
    .geom_line(aes(color=c.name))
)









The four storms are spread across three months. Dennis comes and goes in July, Katrina and Rita overlap in the same terrible fortnight at the end of August, and Wilma, the strongest of the four, does not even begin until October.

If a line can connect a storm’s wind speeds in order, it ought to be able to connect its positions in order. Try it: take Katrina again and draw her track, longitude against latitude, with geom_line. Look closely at what comes back and explain what the geometry has done.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_line()
)









Answer: The track has been replaced by a sawtooth. The line geometry does not connect the rows in the order they appear in the data; it connects them in order from left to right along the x-axis. For wind against doy that is the same thing, because the day of the year only ever increases. Longitude does not. Katrina ran west across Florida into the Gulf and then curved back to the northeast, so she visited the same longitudes twice, and the geometry has stitched her early points to her late ones. Use a line when the x-axis is time, or something else that only moves one way. Longitude on a map can double back, so last week’s track had to be points.

Bars. Using the peak table from question 5, draw one bar per storm whose length is that storm’s peak wind speed. Put the name on the x-axis and the wind on the y-axis, then add .coord_flip() so the names are readable.



View code
(
    peak
    .ggplot(aes(c.name, c.wind))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)









The bars come out neatly ranked, strongest at the bottom, and the four storms that dominated the season separate themselves from the other seventeen at a glance. Nothing in the plotting code asked for that ranking. Where did it come from?
Sort peak alphabetically and draw exactly the same plot again.


View code
(
    peak
    .sort(c.name)
    .ggplot(aes(c.name, c.wind))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)









Answer: The bars are drawn in the order the rows appear in the table. The first plot was ranked by wind because peak still carried the sort from question 5, and the second is alphabetical because we just re-sorted it. The geometry has no opinion about which order is right; it takes the one you hand it. You choose the order of the bars whether or not you notice, and .sort() lets you choose it deliberately. Chapter 7 returns to this with categories whose order depends on a summary of the group itself, such as its count or its median, rather than on a column you can sort directly.

Any geometry can be given its own dataset with the data= argument, which is the standard way to make one part of a plot stand out from the rest. Draw all the 2005 tracks as faint points, then draw Katrina’s track on top of them in "#F5276C" with her name beside her peak. You will need to save Katrina’s rows to a variable first, and you can reuse peak for the label by filtering it.



View code
katrina = (
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
)
katrina_peak = (
    peak
    .filter(c.name == "Katrina")
)

(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.2)
    .geom_point(color="#F5276C", data=katrina)
    .geom_text(
        aes(label=c.name),
        color="#F5276C",
        nudge_y=2.5,
        size=10,
        data=katrina_peak
    )
)










Every plot so far has been labeled with raw column names, which is fine while you are the only person looking. This one is worth showing to someone else. Take the previous plot and add a .labs() layer giving the axes real names and the plot a title.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.2)
    .geom_point(color="#F5276C", data=katrina)
    .geom_text(
        aes(label=c.name),
        color="#F5276C",
        nudge_y=2.5,
        size=10,
        data=katrina_peak
    )
    .labs(
        x="Longitude",
        y="Latitude",
        title="The 2005 Atlantic hurricane season",
        subtitle="Katrina's track shown in pink"
    )
)

Questions
This week’s data is the hundred highest grossing films in the United States in each year from 1970 to 2019, which makes 5,000 rows. Each row is one film. The gross column is domestic box office in millions of dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so the numbers rise over the fifty years for reasons that have nothing to do with how many tickets were sold. The rating is the IMDb user score out of ten and rating_count is how many people voted; metacritic is a critic score out of a hundred; mpa is the rating label (G, PG, R, and so on) and runtime is in minutes.
Last time the table was complete and every group had something in it. This one is full of holes. This notebook is mostly about counting, and the interesting thing about a count is what it does not include. Several questions below group by decade, which is not a column in the data. Build it with integer division, as in (c.year // 10) * 10.
Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it to a variable.

Add a decade column and count the films in each decade in three ways: with pl.len(), and with .count() on the rating column and on metacritic. Then say what the three numbers are counting.

Metacritic did not launch until 2001. Everything before it was scored later, if anyone got around to it, and mostly nobody did.

There are 495 films with no recorded gross at all. Polars sorts nulls to the top of a descending sort, so .first() handed us a film with no box office instead of the largest one. (The 1970s answer, a 1971 film called Grease with a 4.6 rating, is not the musical. It is a different film that happens to share the name, which is question 3 coming back to bite.) Dropping the missing grosses first gives Star Wars, E.T., Titanic, Avatar, and The Force Awakens, and now the two columns agree. The bug was easy to catch only because the right answers are famous enough to make the wrong ones obvious. Most bugs will not give themselves away like that.
